clinicalPearls: Accidental hypothermia is defined as an unintentional fall in core temperature below 35C (95F); at this threshold the compensatory mechanisms that conserve heat begin to fail. Primary hypothermia follows direct cold exposure of a previously healthy person, while secondary hypothermia complicates a systemic illness or injury and carries a much higher mortality.

Core temperature cannot be reliably predicted from the clinical picture, so confirmation requires direct measurement; a probe in the lower third of the esophagus with continuous monitoring is preferred because rectal and bladder readings lag behind true core changes.

Severity grading by core temperature: mild 35C to 32.2C (initial tachycardia then bradycardia, shivering, apathy, dysarthria, impaired judgment, cold diuresis); moderate 32.2C to 28C (declining consciousness, pupillary dilation, paradoxical undressing, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias, J-wave changes, loss of protective airway reflexes); severe below 28C (coma, loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole, apnea, poikilothermia).

Vital signs are difficult to interpret without the core temperature: respiratory rate should be low because CO2 production declines, so persistent hyperventilation suggests a CNS lesion or organic acidosis, and tachycardia out of proportion to temperature suggests secondary causes such as hypoglycemia, hypovolemia, or toxin overdose.

Paradoxical undressing (inappropriate removal of clothing in response to cold stress) is a classic maladaptive behavior; cold-induced ileus and rectus abdominis spasm can mimic or mask an acute abdomen, and confusion or combativeness resolves faster with rewarming than with chemical or physical restraint.
The J (Osborn) wave at the QRS-ST junction supports the diagnosis and is frequently misread by automated ECG software as an injury current.

Laboratory values are systematically distorted by cold: hematocrit rises about 2% per 1C drop (masking anemia), white-cell sequestration and marrow suppression can mask infection, and coagulation tests run at 37C appear deceptively normal despite a genuine in-vivo coagulopathy, so platelet and fresh-frozen-plasma transfusion is ineffective for the cold-induced coagulopathy.

Arterial blood gases should NOT be temperature-corrected; an uncorrected pH of 7.42 and PCO2 of 40 mmHg reflect appropriate ventilation and acid-base balance at any core temperature, and overzealous hyperventilation is a common error given depressed CO2 production.

Frostbite occurs when tissue temperature falls below 0C (32F): ice-crystal formation distorts cellular architecture, endothelial damage produces microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing there is progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, edema, and superficial necrosis, with mummification and demarcation taking weeks to months.

Frostbite always produces a sensory deficit (light touch, pain, or temperature); superficial frostbite causes anesthesia and erythema without tissue loss, whereas vesiculation with surrounding edema/erythema indicates deeper injury and hemorrhagic vesicles signal severe microvascular damage that may lead to amputation.

Chilblain (pernio) is a nonfreezing injury from repetitive damp-cold exposure above freezing, most common in young women with a history of Raynaud phenomenon, producing erythema, edema, pruritus, then plaques, blue nodules, and ulcerations on the dorsa of hands and feet.

Trench foot / immersion foot results from repetitive wet-cold exposure above freezing; feet are initially cyanotic, cold, and edematous, with bullae progressing to ulceration and liquefaction gangrene, and survivors may have hyperhidrosis, cold sensitivity, and painful ambulation for years.
harrison.pathophysiology: Heat is lost by radiation (55-65%), conduction (10-15%, markedly increased in cold water), convection (increased with wind), respiration, and evaporation. The preoptic anterior hypothalamus orchestrates thermoregulation: the immediate autonomic defense releases norepinephrine, raises muscle tone, and triggers shivering to increase the basal metabolic rate, while cutaneous cold reception drives reflex vasoconstriction; prolonged cold also stimulates the thyroid axis. When these defenses are overwhelmed, hypothermia first stimulates and then progressively depresses every organ system. In peripheral freezing injury, tissue freezing causes ice-crystal formation that destroys cellular architecture; endothelial damage leads to stasis and microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, rising tissue pressures, edema, and necrosis develop. Nonfreezing injuries (chilblain, trench/immersion foot) arise from neuronal and endothelial damage caused by repetitive cold exposure above the freezing point.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis (hypothermia is a poor prognostic sign)
Diabetic ketoacidosis and other metabolic acidoses
CNS injury (cerebrovascular accident, subarachnoid hemorrhage, hypothalamic lesion, spinal cord injury)
Shapiro syndrome (agenesis of corpus callosum with episodic hypothermia)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cold-induced ileus with rectus abdominis spasm mimicking an acute abdomen
Areflexia attributed to hypothermia masking a spinal cord lesion
J (Osborn) waves misinterpreted as an injury current / ischemia
Trench/immersion foot bullae indistinguishable from frostbite
Shaking rigors of infection mistaken for shivering
additionalInvestigations: Continuous core temperature monitoring, ideally esophageal (lower third); rectal/bladder as ancillary
ECG (look for J/Osborn wave, bradydysrhythmias, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias)
Arterial blood gas read uncorrected for temperature
Serum potassium (prognostic in arrest), glucose, electrolytes, renal function
Coagulation studies, fibrinogen, and platelet count (interpret with caution)
Hematocrit (artificially elevated by cold) and white-cell count
Bedside echocardiography and end-tidal CO2 to confirm perfusion status
For frostbite: angiography, fluorescence microangiography, technetium-99 / pyrophosphate bone scan, or MR angiography to assess tissue viability and demarcation
redFlags: Core temperature below 28C (severe): coma, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole
Potassium >12 mmol/L during resuscitation indicates widespread cell lysis and grave prognosis
Core temperature <10-12C, pH <6.5, or fibrinogen <0.5 g/L may preclude continued resuscitation
Hypothermia complicating sepsis is a poor prognostic sign
Asphyxia preceding cooling (e.g., avalanche burial) is the strongest negative predictor of survival
Hemorrhagic vesicles or persistent cyanosis after rewarming in frostbite (risk of amputation, compartment syndrome)
Frostbite with rhabdomyolysis and completely frozen extremities
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on whether hypothermia is primary or secondary, the precipitating cause, and the presence of asphyxia. Secondary hypothermia complicating systemic illness carries much higher mortality, and hypothermia with sepsis is a poor prognostic sign. Because cold itself is protective, survival has been reported after cardiac arrest times exceeding 7 hours, and intact neurologic recovery has occurred at extremely low core temperatures; the patient is not dead until warm and dead. Markers of a grave prognosis during resuscitation include potassium >12 mmol/L (cell lysis), pH <6.5, fibrinogen <0.5 g/L, and core temperature <10-12C, while preceding asphyxia (avalanche) is the most important negative predictor. The HOPE score uses six covariates to predict which arrested hypothermic patients may benefit from extracorporeal life support. Frostbite sequelae often persist as paresthesia, thermal misperception, and hyperhidrosis, with delayed nail deformities, cutaneous carcinomas, and epiphyseal damage in children.
pitfalls: Correcting arterial blood gases for temperature; the uncorrected values guide management
Overzealous hyperventilation despite depressed CO2 production, dangerously raising pH
Applying direct heat to extremities in chronic severe hypothermia, which causes peripheral vasodilation and core 'afterdrop'
Transfusing platelets or fresh-frozen plasma for the cold coagulopathy (ineffective, as the defect is temperature-dependent enzyme inhibition)
Deep insertion of central venous catheters or pulmonary artery catheters into the cold heart, which can precipitate refractory arrhythmias or perforation
Trusting coagulation tests or hematocrit at face value (assays run at 37C; hematocrit falsely elevated)
Premature termination of frostbite thawing because reperfusion is intensely painful
Repeated dosing of drugs (e.g., digoxin, insulin) that are ineffective while cold but become toxic during rewarming
harrison.severityClassification: Hypothermia is graded by core temperature: Mild = 35C (95F) to 32.2C (90F); Moderate = below 32.2C (90F) to 28C (82.4F); Severe = below 28C (82.4F). Frostbite is classified as superficial (anesthesia and erythema, no tissue loss) versus deep (vesiculation, hemorrhagic vesicles, possible amputation); an alternative scheme grades by the proximal extent of presenting cyanosis: grade 1 none, grade 2 distal phalanx, grade 3 to the metacarpophalangeal joint, grade 4 proximal to the MP joint.
